With its late ‘70s style circuit and symmetrical hard clipping, it’s EHX’s take on the RAT2™ pedal, only we think it’s better. The Flatiron Fuzz is extremely versatile. At lower drive settings it remains fairly clean and adds a pleasing mild distortion. As the drive is turned up it transports you to a world of arena rock and produces spectacular, thick, meaty tones. The stellar sound of the Flatiron Fuzz is a result of its classic, late ‘70s style circuitry and the fact that it delivers symmetrical hard clipping. As a point of reference, you might refer to the old Rat pedal, but we think you’ll prefer the Flatiron. The Flatiron Fuzz features three controls: Volume, Drive and Filter. Volume sets the output level while Drive adjusts the amount of sustain and distortion. The unique Filter control is actually a low pass filter with a movable cut-off frequency. This is especially cool because it lets you dial in just the right amount of high-end… from dark to raunchy. Electro-Harmonix trivia: The Flatiron Fuzz is named after the historic Flatiron Building in New York City. It’s an iconic landmark located just down the block from EHX headquarters in the 1970s and it’s the building pictured on the pedal. The RAT2 is a trademark of Act Audio. sources.excerpt: User manual Electro Harmonix Flatiron Fuzz (English - 2 pages) Manua . ls Manua . ls Electro Harmonix effect machines · Electro Harmonix Flatiron Fuzz manual 7.5 · 1 give review PDF manual · 2 pages English tutorial questions specs Electro Harmonix Flatiron Fuzz FLATIRON FUZZ Congratulations on your purchase of the Flatiron Fuzz, an extremely versatile, classic op-amp powered pedal that can take you all the way from warm, round overdrive to full-on, fuzzy distortion. At lower drive settings the Flatiron Fuzz will remain fairly clean adding a pleasant mild drive. At medium and higher drive settings the Flatiron Fuzz can produce a thick classic tone circa the late ‘ 70s and far beyond. The expressive filter lets you dial in just the right amount of high- end...from dark to raunchy. The Flatiron Fuzz features true bypass. Electro-Harmonix trivia: the Flatiron Fuzz is named after the historic Flatiron Building in New York City. It’s an iconic landmark located just down the block from EHX headquarters in the 1970s and it’s the building pictured on your pedal. OPERATING INSTRUCTIONS DRI VE Knob — Controls the amount of input gain that goes into the fuzz circuit. Turn the DRIVE clockwise to go from clean to high gain. FILTER Knob — Sets a low pass filter that tames the natural highs that are accentuated by the fuzz circuit. As the FILTER knob is turned clockwise, the filter’s frequency increases allowing more high-end to pass through the pedal. VOL Knob — Adjusts the output volume of the Flatiron Fuzz. FOOTSWITCH and LED — The footswitch toggles the Flatiron Fuzz between effect and true bypass mode. The LED lights when the effect is engaged. INPUT Jack — This 1/4” jack is the input to the Flatiron Fuzz. Plug your guitar into here. The input impedance is 1MOhm. AMP Jack — This 1/4” jack is the Flatiron Fuzz ’s output. Connect this to the input of your next effect or amplifier. Output impedance varies from 500 Ohms to 25KOhms depending on the VOL Knob setting. POWER The Flatiron Fuzz can run off of a 9V battery or you can use an optional 9VDC AC Adapter capable of delivering at least 25mA to the 9V power jack, such as the EHX9.6DC- 200. The AC Adapter must have a center negative plug. The battery may be left in or taken out when using an AC Adapter. The Flatiron Fuzz has a current draw of 5mA at 9VDC. Need help? sources.h1: Quick Hit Electro-Harmonix Flatiron Fuzz Review: A Precision-Cut, Low-Noise Fuzz Pedal for Modern Players
sources.excerpt: Quick Hit Electro-Harmonix Flatiron Fuzz Review: A Precision-Cut, Low-Noise Fuzz Pedal for Modern Players | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / gear reviews gear reviews Quick Hit Electro-Harmonix Flatiron Fuzz Review: A Precision-Cut, Low-Noise Fuzz Pedal for Modern Players By Liam Carter July 11, 2026 First Impressions and Core Philosophy Electro-Harmonix’s Flatiron Fuzz is not another reissue of a ’60s circuit nor a saturated octave-doubling monster—it’s a deliberate, modern reinterpretation of silicon-based fuzz that prioritizes clarity, dynamic response, and low-noise operation without sacrificing harmonic richness. Released in Q2 2023, the Flatiron sits alongside EHX’s Canyon and Oceans 11 in their ‘Precision Tone’ series, sharing design DNA with tight voltage regulation, ultra-low-noise op-amps (Texas Instruments OPA2134), and discrete silicon transistors (Fairchild KSP13/2N5088 complementary pair). At $179 MSRP, it competes directly with the Wampler Tumnus Deluxe ($199), EarthQuaker Devices Hummingbird ($189), and JHS Angry Charlie V3 ($199), but distinguishes itself via a unique dual-stage gain architecture and a proprietary clipping scheme that avoids traditional diode saturation. Housed in a rugged, powder-coated steel chassis measuring 4.75" × 2.5" × 1.75", the Flatiron weighs 328 g—noticeably heavier than the average 220–260 g stompbox due to its reinforced internal PCB mounting and oversized aluminum footswitch (Korg-style momentary switch rated for 10 million cycles). The layout features three knobs—Volume, Fuzz, and Tone—with a fourth toggle labeled 'Mode' offering Clean Blend or Sustain Boost. Unlike many contemporary fuzzes, there’s no bias control, no gate, and no external power jack: it runs exclusively on 9V DC (center-negative) with a regulated internal 5.1V rail, eliminating battery sag artifacts entirely. Technical Architecture and Circuit Design Silicon Transistor Pairing and Gain Staging The Flatiron employs a cascaded two-stage silicon transistor amplifier, using matched Fairchild KSP13 NPN and 2N5088 PNP transistors in a Class-A common-emitter configuration. Each stage operates at 3.2 mA collector current, verified via multimeter probing at test points TP1 and TP2 on the production board (rev. B2). This deliberate bias point delivers symmetrical clipping while minimizing thermal drift—measured drift was just ±0.8 mV/°C across a 15°C–40°C ambient range during accelerated aging tests. Stage one provides raw gain (up to 38 dB measured at 1 kHz with Fuzz at 3 o’clock), while stage two applies dynamic compression and soft clipping via a proprietary dual-junction network—not standard 1N4148 or LED clippers.
